solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid

annotation.surface: Someone feels gloomy on a morning without their usual tabloid.
annotation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse clue order: 'without the Sun' is SUN then LESS. The question mark flags that the newspaper is also the thing in the sky.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the weather sense: with no sunshine the day is dark and dreary.

indicatorNotes.horrible: something horrible is a mess, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters including the S of the possessive

annotation.surface: A complaint about the dreadful food served in an American canteen.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S looks like a possessive, but its S is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers anything eaten or drunk to keep the body going, which is what food does.

entries.clue: Sir Lancelot perhaps losing head in time of darkness (5)

indicatorNotes.losing head: a head is the top of a thing, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: Sir Lancelot is an example of a knight

annotation.surface: An Arthurian knight is beheaded under cover of dark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' means Lancelot is just one example of the category wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the hours between dusk and dawn are the daily period without light.

entries.clue: Thoughtful after Conservative’s last vote? It could be costly (9)

indicatorNotes.last: the final letter of the word before it is taken
indicatorNotes.after: the thoughtful word comes after the other pieces in the answer

blocks.note: you mark a ballot paper with an X

annotation.surface: A voter muses over a Conservative vote and wonders what it might cost.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you PENSIVE goes at the end even though it comes first in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something with a high price.

blocks.note: an adjective meaning neat and smart in appearance
the conifer traditionally brought indoors at Christmas

annotation.surface: A Christmas tree decked out in its finery.
annotation.walkthrough: The tree is literally dressed with decorations, which ties the two meanings together.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: an adjective for someone smartly turned out, and the Norway spruce, the classic Christmas tree.

entries.clue: Forest dweller a tiresome customer, they say (4)

indicatorNotes.they say: what people say is heard, so it points to how a word sounds

blocks.note: a tiresome person is a bore; the answer shares its sound

annotation.surface: Gossip that a woodland character is dull company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Customer' here just means a person, as in 'a tricky customer'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the wild pig is one of many animals living in woodland.

entries.clue: I don’t think much of this unfinished work by writer (3)

annotation.definition: I don’t think much of this

indicatorNotes.unfinished: a thing unfinished lacks its end, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a book is a work by a writer

annotation.surface: A critic dismisses an incomplete piece by an author.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole spoken remark, the kind of thing a jeering audience means.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the jeer shouted at a poor performance says exactly 'I don't think much of this'.

entries.clue: Greed putting drunken vicar in A&E (7)

indicatorNotes.drunken: a drunk staggers about, so the letters are jumbled
indicatorNotes.putting: with 'in', an instruction to place one thing inside another
indicatorNotes.in: the jumbled word goes inside A&E

blocks.note: the letters A and E, split to hold the rest

annotation.surface: A drunk vicar ends up in hospital casualty, and greed is somehow to blame.
annotation.walkthrough: A&E (Accident and Emergency) is the British hospital casualty department; here it just supplies its two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an excessive desire for money or possessions.

indicatorNotes.reversed: turned round, so read the word backwards

annotation.surface: A news line about a dip in American fuel prices.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slump in US petrol' reads as one phrase; 'in' is only the link.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to sink or droop, and both are used of prices or trade falling off.

indicatorNotes.seizing: the words grab hold of the answer, which sits inside them

annotation.surface: Kidnappers on the Portuguese coast grab someone.
annotation.walkthrough: The kidnapping story makes 'seizing' look literal; it is the wordplay that does the seizing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as adjectives: belonging to or affecting one particular person.

entries.clue: Act calmly and lay co-pilot off (4,2,4)

indicatorNotes.off: something off has gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: Advice to a captain: stay calm and sack the co-pilot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lay off' looks like a phrasal verb meaning dismiss, which hides that 'off' is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to stay outwardly relaxed and unbothered, especially under pressure.

entries.clue: Perhaps John’s lonely at first in exclusive school (5)

indicatorNotes.at first: only the beginning of the word is taken, its first letter
indicatorNotes.in: the letter goes inside the school

blocks.note: Eton is an expensive English private school

annotation.surface: A boy named John is lonely at a posh boarding school.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition points at the singer: the answer is a name that can come before John. 'Perhaps' marks it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Sir Elton John is one famous John, and this is his first name.

indicatorNotes.wearing: the outer word is worn around the letters like clothing, so they go inside it

annotation.surface: An amiable duke and a companion dressed in pink.
annotation.walkthrough: The duke and the one both wear the pink, so the two letters go in together.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: warm and pleasant in manner.

entries.clue: Speak on behalf of Royal Engineers in attendance (9)

blocks.note: RE = Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

annotation.surface: A spokesperson for the Royal Engineers turns up to speak.
annotation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers are a corps of the British Army, very often RE in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a lawyer or an MP acts and speaks for others.

indicatorNotes.in: the cold letter goes inside the lorry word

blocks.note: an artic is an articulated lorry
C = cold, as on a tap

annotation.surface: A driver complains that the lorry cab is freezing.
annotation.walkthrough: ARTIC is British slang for an articulated lorry, a large truck with a separate trailer. Oink uses 'cold' twice on purpose: once for C, once in the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Extended from the polar region: anything as cold as the far north.

entries.clue: West African country booting out an old prime minister (7)

indicatorNotes.booting out: kicking something out of the word, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: O = old, removed from the country

annotation.surface: A West African nation expels a former prime minister.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old' is the letter booted out, so it cannot also be part of the definition, though it reads as if it were.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: David Cameron was British prime minister from 2010 to 2016.

indicatorNotes.into: one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: STUDY emptied of its middle leaves S and Y
peed = went, as in went to the toilet

annotation.surface: Someone hurried into an empty study.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Went' reads as walked; the setter means the lavatorial sense. 'Empty' removes all the inside letters of study.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: moving or happening quickly.

entries.clue: Actor in study with press, scratching bottom (2,4)

indicatorNotes.scratching bottom: to scratch is to strike off, and the bottom of a down entry is its last letter

blocks.note: to iron clothes is to press them

annotation.surface: An actor sits in his study with a newspaper, scratching his backside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Press' suggests newspapers, but here it is the verb for smoothing clothes.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Robert De Niro is one of the best-known film actors.

indicatorNotes.excluded from: shut out of the word, so that letter is removed

annotation.surface: A Liberal is barred from a whole competition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contest' looks like a noun; it is the verb, to match the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to take part in a struggle for a prize.

entries.clue: Order detective inspector to appear in English court (5)

indicatorNotes.to appear in: the detective turns up inside the court, so those letters go inside the others

blocks.note: DI = detective inspector, a police rank

annotation.surface: A detective inspector is ordered to attend an English court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order' reads as an instruction to the detective, but it is the definition, a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a decree issued by someone in authority.

annotation.surface: A judge on an island has lost his temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Judge' is the verb, not the person in the wig.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from Latin ira, anger: stronger than cross, closer to furious.

indicatorNotes.in: the area letter goes inside the jumbled letters
indicatorNotes.strange: the letters are made strange, so rearranged

annotation.surface: An official has to run an area in unfamiliar parts.
annotation.walkthrough: The jumble of regions has to be chosen so that A can sit in the middle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to arrange and run things efficiently.

indicatorNotes.periodically: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

annotation.surface: A fool keeps stopping every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pauses periodically' reads as a description of the idiot, but it is the letter source.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the donkey's name has long been used for a stupid person.

indicatorNotes.initially: at the start, so only the word's first letter is used

annotation.surface: An instruction to step back and vanish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back away' reads as one verb, but 'Back' is the definition, as in 'years back'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for time past: two years ago, two years back.

annotation.surface: A reminder that the responsibility falls on you and me.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nearly spells the answer out: the duty falls on us.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Latin for load: the duty or burden of doing something.

annotation.surface: Someone who makes porridge goes without at suppertime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Porridge-maker' sounds like a cook, but it is the stuff porridge is made from.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-style description: ground oats are what porridge is made from, so they are its maker.
